newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan steps up aid, investment in central Asia.
newsitem.headline: Japan steps up aid, investment in central Asia.

text.p: Japan, the world's largest provider of aid to developing nations, is directing more assistance to central Asia, one of the most promising areas in the region, government officials say.

And encouraged by the government's growing commitment to the area, major Japanese commercial banks are considering establishing a presence in central Asia to tap the region's business opportunities, bankers say.
Central Asia, which includes countries that form part of the former Soviet Union, is hoping to get not only more financial assistance from Japan but also intellectual and technical expertise.

The Japanese government, faced with shrinking growth in foreign aid amid a budget shortfall, is beginning to concentrate its aid and diversify the forms of assistance. It is moving away from providing just money alone.
"Assistance (to central Asia) is becoming important to the national interest," said a senior official at the Finance Ministry's institute of fiscal and monetary policy.
The development of central Asia, which is rich in natural resources such as gas and oil, would be of strategic importance to Japan, which meets most of its energy needs through imports.
Central Asian nations comprise Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, and Turkmenistan.
They have been moving towards a market economy since the dismantling of the Soviet empire in 1991 and have called upon Japan to support the process, said the ministry official.

This month, the Japanese Finance Ministry helped set up a financial training institute in Uzbekistan in a bid to help that country improve the management of its financial sector and develop specialists in such areas as monetary policy.
A high-ranking ministry official is now there to help run the institute. "This is the first of this kind of assistance," said the ministry official.
The prime minister of Uzbekistan plans to visit Japan this December and will meet Japanese officials as well as business executives, he added.

Japanese official development assistance (ODA) stood at $14.73 billion in calendar 1995, up nine percent from the $13.47 billion in the previous year. And of the 1995 amount, $67 million went to central Asian nations, up 37 percent from the $49 million in 1994.

Japan is sympathetic towards central Asian nations' attempts to adopt reforms gradually, instead of taking the go-fast approach which has severely disrupted the economies of some developing countries, officials say.
"The economic and political stability of those nations is vital because they are surrounded by diplomatically important countries such as Russia and China," said an official at the foreign ministry.
The Japanese private sector is also now looking at central Asia for new business opportunities.

"Major Japanese banks are now considering making inroads into central Asia as some Japanese trading firms are already conducting operations there," said an official at the international planning division of a leading Japanese bank.
"That will mark a departure for us," he added.
The Japanese government is trying to promote private-sector investment in central Asia by easing rules on Japanese banks operating there.
Before, Japanese banks were required to set aside special reserves in case nations there could not repay their loans.
But last month the Japanese government notified banks that they no longer needed to set aside special loan-loss reserves.
As a result, Japanese commercial banks have now been given more freedom to expand their exposure in central Asia.
